title: Why You'd Never Survive on Venus
screen_title: Why You'd Never Survive on Venus
subtitle: Earth's twin is the deadliest planet next door
yt_title: Why You'd Never Survive on Venus
intro: What would happen if you landed on Venus, the planet that looks like Earth's twin? We drop through clouds of acid, feel air heavy enough to crush a submarine, stand on ground hot enough to melt lead, and find out how long the toughest machines ever built lasted down there. Stay to the end for the one place on Venus where you could actually survive.
questions: Would you rather visit Venus or Mars?
Would you live in a floating city above Venus?
What should we never visit next?
tags: what if you landed on venus

segments.text: What if you stepped out onto Venus? You'd be crushed, cooked and choked, all in the same second. Your spacesuit wouldn't save you. Neither would a tank. So how long could anything last down there?
Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we fall through the clouds of Earth's twin. So, let's go.

files: Good Morning From the International Space Station.jpg
visual.query: Good Morning From the International Space Station

segments.text: Look up just after sunset, and you'll often see it. The brightest thing in the sky after the Moon. A calm, white jewel. That's Venus.
segments.headline: The evening star

segments.text: It's almost the same size as Earth. Almost the same mass. It's our closest planetary neighbor. For centuries, people imagined it as a warm, swampy world full of life.
segments.headline: Earth's twin

segments.text: They were wrong. Venus is the most hostile planet in the solar system. And today, you're going to find out why, layer by layer, from the top of its clouds all the way to the ground.
segments.headline: The deadliest planet

segments.text: And stay to the end, because there is one place on Venus where you could actually take off your heavy suit and breathe easy. Well, almost.

files: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz.jpg
visual.query: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz

segments.headline: One safe place?

segments.text: First, the trip. Venus is the easiest planet to reach. At its closest, it's about forty million kilometers away. A spacecraft can get there in about four to six months.

As you approach, you see no oceans, no continents, no mountains. Just a smooth, creamy ball of cloud, glowing in the sunlight. Venus reflects about three quarters of the light that hits it. That's why it shines so brightly.
segments.headline: A world wrapped in cloud

segments.text: Those clouds never break. Not once, not anywhere. You could orbit Venus for a lifetime and never see the ground with your own eyes.
Now we start falling. About seventy kilometers up, you hit the top of the clouds. And here's the first shock. These aren't water clouds. They're made of droplets of sulfuric acid.
segments.headline: Clouds of acid

segments.text: The same acid in a car battery, only stronger. It would eat through fabric, rubber and skin. Any rain that falls from these clouds is acid rain. But it never reaches the ground. It's far too hot down there. The drops boil away on the way down.

visual.label: what Venus's clouds are made of
visual.sub: it rains, but never reaches the ground

segments.text: And the winds up here are wild. At the cloud tops, they blow at around three hundred and sixty kilometers an hour. Faster than any hurricane on Earth. They whip all the way around the planet in about four days.
segments.headline: Hurricane winds

segments.text: That's strange, because the planet underneath turns incredibly slowly. More on that in a moment.
Keep falling. Below the clouds, the sky turns a murky orange. And the air keeps getting thicker. And thicker. And thicker.
segments.headline: Thicker and thicker

segments.text: By the time you reach the ground, the air pressure is about ninety-two times what you feel on Earth.
To feel that on Earth, you'd have to dive about nine hundred meters under the sea. That's deep enough to crush many submarines.

files: ISS-45 StoryOfWater, Great Barrier Reef, Australia.jpg
visual.query: ISS-45 StoryOfWater, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

segments.headline: 900 m under the sea

segments.text: The air is so dense, it behaves almost like a liquid. Walking would feel like wading through water. A gentle breeze would push you like a strong ocean current.
And you couldn't breathe it. It's about ninety-six percent carbon dioxide, with almost no oxygen at all.
Quick question for you. If you had to pick one planet to visit, Venus or Mars, which would it be? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you rather visit Venus or Mars?

segments.text: Now the heat. Venus is almost twice as far from the Sun as Mercury. Yet it's the hottest planet in the solar system.

files: The Sun by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly of NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory - 20100819.jpg
visual.query: The Sun by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly of NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory - 20100819

segments.headline: Hotter than Mercury

segments.text: On the surface, it's about four hundred and sixty-five degrees Celsius. Day and night. At the poles and at the equator. There's no cool place to hide.
That's hot enough to melt lead. Hotter than a pizza oven. If you dropped a tin spoon on the ground, it would melt into a puddle.
segments.headline: Lead would melt

segments.text: Why so hot? All that carbon dioxide works like a giant blanket. Sunlight gets in, warms the ground, but the heat can't get back out. It's the greenhouse effect, gone completely out of control.
segments.headline: A runaway greenhouse

segments.text: Scientists think Venus may once have had oceans, long ago. As the Sun grew brighter, they evaporated. The water vapor trapped even more heat, and the planet never cooled down again.
segments.headline: Lost oceans

segments.chapter: So how long would you last?
segments.text: So, what would actually happen to you? Let's be honest. In an ordinary spacesuit, you'd be crushed and cooked within moments. The suit would collapse, and the heat would pour in.

files: Ed White First American Spacewalker - GPN-2000-001180.jpg
visual.query: Ed White First American Spacewalker - GPN-2000-001180

segments.headline: Your suit fails

segments.text: Even our toughest machines can't last. In the 1970s and 1980s, the Soviet Union sent a series of landers called Venera. They were built like armored diving bells, packed with cooling systems.
segments.headline: The Venera landers

segments.text: In 1970, Venera 7 became the first spacecraft ever to land on another planet and send back a signal. It lasted about twenty minutes.

The record holder, Venera 13, landed in 1982. It sent back the first color pictures from the surface. A flat, orange plain of rocks under a yellow sky. Then, after about two hours, it went silent. It was cooked.
No spacecraft has touched the surface of Venus since the 1980s. It's that hard.
Now imagine you could survive. You'd notice something odd. Venus spins backwards compared to almost every other planet. So on Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
segments.headline: The Sun rises in the west

segments.text: And it spins incredibly slowly. One turn takes two hundred and forty-three Earth days. But one trip around the Sun takes only two hundred and twenty-five days. So a day on Venus is longer than its year.
Not that you'd see the Sun anyway. Through the thick clouds, it would just be a dim, blurry glow in an orange sky.
And there may be lightning in those clouds, and volcanoes on the ground. Venus has more volcanoes than any other planet. Radar has found signs that some may still be erupting today.
segments.headline: Living volcanoes?

segments.text: And on the tops of its highest mountains, radar sees something shiny. Scientists think it may be a kind of metal frost. Metals that boil off in the lowland heat, then settle as a glittering coat on the cooler peaks.
segments.headline: Metal snow

segments.text: Imagine that. A world so hot, its mountains are dusted not with snow, but with metal.

segments.chapter: The one place you could survive
segments.text: So here's the payoff I promised. Is there anywhere on Venus you could survive? Surprisingly, yes. Not on the ground. In the sky.

files: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz.jpg
visual.query: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz

segments.headline: Up in the sky

segments.text: About fifty to fifty-five kilometers above the surface, the air pressure is almost the same as at sea level on Earth. And the temperature is somewhere between zero and fifty degrees Celsius. Like a warm day at home.

visual.label: Earth-like pressure and temperature
visual.sub: the most Earth-like place beyond Earth

segments.text: It gets better. The air you breathe, oxygen and nitrogen, is lighter than Venus's carbon dioxide. So a big balloon full of ordinary breathable air would float there, all by itself.

files: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz.jpg
visual.query: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz

segments.headline: Air is a lifting gas

segments.text: Some scientists have dreamed of floating cities, drifting with the winds above the clouds. You'd still need an air mask and acid-proof clothes. But you wouldn't need a pressure suit. You could stand outside in light protective gear.
segments.headline: Floating cities

segments.text: So here's my question. Would you live in a floating city, fifty kilometers above Venus, with acid clouds below you? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you live in a floating city above Venus?

segments.text: Venus is also a warning. Two planets, born the same size, from the same materials, side by side. One became a blue world full of life. The other became a furnace.
segments.headline: Two twins, two fates

segments.text: That's why space agencies are planning new missions to Venus. They want to know what went wrong, and whether Venus was ever a place where life could have started.
So the next time you see that bright evening star, remember. It's beautiful from here. And it's the last place in the solar system you'd ever want to land.
